newsitem.title: USA: INSTANT VIEW -- U.S. Jan retail sales up 0.6 pct.
newsitem.headline: INSTANT VIEW -- U.S. Jan retail sales up 0.6 pct.

text.p: Following are comments from U.S. economists after the Commerce Department reported retail sales rose 0.6 percent in January compared to a revised 0.3 percent jump in December.
The ex-auto indicator rose 0.4 percent in January against a revised unchanged reading the previous month.
U.S. economists in a Reuters survey had expected overall retail sales to be up 0.7 percent.
ALLAN LESLIE, INDEPENDENT ECONOMIST, NEW YORK:
"I think what it is is really the apparel number dropping 0.9 percent."

Speaking on Reuters Financial Television, Leslie added: "I believe that this sort of puts yet another nail in the coffin" of hopes for a Federal Reserve tightening of monetary policy near term. Leslie said he expected the Fed to continue its steady policy course, while maintaining an asymmetrical directive with a bias toward tighter credit.
ALAN LEVENSON, MONEY MARKET ECONOMIST, UBS SECURITIES INC:
"It wasn't very far from most people's estimates and probably won't change anyone's outlook. Do note (though) that there were net downward revisions for December."
MICHAEL NIEMIRA, ECONOMIST, BANK OF TOKYO-MITSUBISHI:

"It's a lot stronger than what we have been seeing ... When you step back, it says the consumer is alive and well and continues to spend. The near-term dynamic is still favorable, but what happens toward the end of the year is a different story. The second half is when we may see a slowdown in consumption."
CHRISTOPHER LOW, SENIOR ECONOMIST, HSBC MARKETS INC:
"(The report) was a touch weaker than expected given the revisions to the prior month."
Low continued: "Ex-auto December figures were revised to unchanged from up 0.6 percent, that was a fairly sharp downward revision. These are is very friendly numbers for the (U.S. Treasury) market.
"You still have some decent consumer spending growth going into the first quarter, but it was not quite what was expected. People were expecting fairly stronger growth.
"I think this is really the best the Fed could hope for this morning given what we already knew about consumer spending in the month," Low concluded.
DONALD MAUDE, CHIEF U.S. ECONOMIST, SCOTIA CAPITAL MARKETS INC:

"The (Treasury) market probably liked the fact that you got a sizeable downward revision to December. You're going to get a downward revision to (Gross Domestic Product) in the fourth quarter (of 1996). They might pull that down to 4.2 percent (from a preliminary estimate of 4.7 percent).

"(The first-quarter economy) looks pretty good. Except for apparel, the sales strength was broad-based. The only thing that was down were apparel sales, but I think that was due to heavy discounting ... Gas station sales may have bloated the number a little because of the higher price of gasoline."
HUGH JOHNSON, CHIEF INVESTMENT OFFICER, FIRST ALBANY CORP:
"The number is pretty much in line with expectations. There's a little more of a revision to December than I thought, but that's not a big deal."

Including the drop in initial weekly jobless claims to 309,000 from 324,000 in the latest week, Johnson said: "My impression of the two numbers is that the first quarter is starting off a little bit stronger than I thought. I had hoped for 2.0 percent growth in the first quarter, and the numbers we have looked at including the employment numbers are hinting at a stronger first quarter."
DAVID WYSS, RESEARCH DIRECTOR, DRI/MCGRAW HILL:

"The 0.6 ... was about what we were expecting after we had the chain store sales from last week. Auto sales we knew were good because we got a very good bounce in car sales. As usual, the retail sales for cars didn't go up as much as the unit sales.

"For the (Treasury) market it's a good number but pretty much in line with expectations. I wouldn't think you'd see much movement. This is a good number for January. We had been a little worried after the durable goods numbers that things were slowing down in the first quarter. This certainly is some contra-indication for that and suggests (the Fed) still need to tighten."
(( -- N.A. Treasury Desk, 212-859-1660 ))
